Example 7.2 — Ligand efficiency over time: BACE1 inhibitors¶

A reproducible record of an AI-assisted BindingDB analysis: each prompt, the BindingDB tool calls that answered it with their recorded results, the answer, and its figures. Run all cells to show the recorded results, or rerun every call on your own copy of the database and check each result against the recorded one.

  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Model: claude-sonnet-5-5
  • Data: BindingDB release 202611 (BDB-mySQL_All_202611_dmp.zip, SHA-256 daea9260d404919a183ce02d91bf4b9c49b410bea7eaaeba105c8e0280510381)
  • Database build: 2026-11-21T01:08:15+00:00, DuckDB 1.5.6
  • Derived data: standard InChIKeys computed from SMILES by RDKit 2026.03.6; compound_property computed from SMILES (largest fragment) by RDKit 2026.03.6
  • Server: mcp-bindingdb v0.1.17, commit 79dae5d22c0f
  • Software: python 3.12.7, duckdb 1.5.6, rdkit 2026.03.6, mcp 2.3.0, gemmi 0.7.5
  • Notebook generated: 2026-11-24T04:56:14Z
  • Contents: 1 exchange · 12 tool calls · 2 figures · 1 code cell

How to run¶

Keep the notebook in its folder, which holds everything it needs: requirements.txt (mcp-bindingdb at its commit and the versions of the packages it needs), the recorded results in data/, the figures in figures/ and the analysis code the notebook imports (plot_bace1_efficiency.py). With uv, from that folder (replace the path with yours):

cd /path/to/7.2-ligand-efficiency-notebook
uv run --no-project --with-requirements requirements.txt --with jupyterlab jupyter lab 7.2-ligand-efficiency-notebook.ipynb

then choose Run → Run All Cells. The first start installs the packages, which takes a minute or two; the cells show the recorded results, so no database is needed. Without uv: pip install -r requirements.txt jupyterlab, then jupyter lab 7.2-ligand-efficiency-notebook.ipynb in the folder.

How to rerun the calls¶

To rerun every BindingDB call on your own copy of release 202611 and check each result against the recorded one, set RERUN = True in the setup cell and run all cells, or rerun the notebook without opening Jupyter, writing a copy with the new results:

cd /path/to/7.2-ligand-efficiency-notebook
BINDINGDB_RERUN=1 uv run --no-project --with-requirements requirements.txt --with nbconvert jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --output 7.2-ligand-efficiency-notebook-rerun.ipynb 7.2-ligand-efficiency-notebook.ipynb

A rerun needs the database: the one BINDINGDB_DUCKDB=/path/to/bindingdb_202611.duckdb names (put it before uv run), else the newest one mcp-bindingdb built on this computer, for example for Claude Desktop. With neither, the first rerun builds one, which takes about half an hour and 2.4 GB. To build exactly release 202611, with a clone of mcp-bindingdb:

git clone https://github.com/sbl-sdsc/mcp-bindingdb.git
cd mcp-bindingdb
git checkout 79dae5d22c0f15b8ded9b49adc8b105f0463703a
scripts/build_duckdb.sh --release 202611

The setup cell checks the database's release and source checksum against the recorded ones.

Run as it is, each call cell shows its recorded result, read from data/ and checked against the SHA-256 digest recorded in the cell. Rerun, it shows the new result with ✅ when it matches the recorded one (floats to 10 significant digits, ids of viewers and files left out). Calls to PubChem, RCSB or PDBe depend on those services and may differ. The prose answers are the model's and are not recomputed. Code cells hold the analysis code the model wrote; they run as written (reading the results with replay.result(n), the result of Call n) and draw their figures again, which are not compared.

In [ ]:
# Shows the results recorded during the session (data/), so the notebook runs without a database. Set
# RERUN = True (or start Jupyter with BINDINGDB_RERUN=1) to rerun every BindingDB call on a local copy of
# the database instead and check it against its recorded result: see 'How to rerun the calls' above.
from mcp_bindingdb.notebook import Replay

RERUN = False
replay = Replay(release='202611', source_zip_sha256='daea9260d404919a183ce02d91bf4b9c49b410bea7eaaeba105c8e0280510381', rerun=RERUN)

Recorded with BindingDB release 202611, mcp-bindingdb v0.1.17 (commit 79dae5d22c0f)
python 3.12.7, duckdb 1.5.6, rdkit 2026.03.6, mcp 2.3.0, gemmi 0.7.5

# Call 5 · run_sql · ran 2026-11-24 04:56:13 UTC
sql = """
    WITH best AS (SELECT monomerid, max(p_affinity) AS p, min(year) AS fy FROM activity
     WHERE polymerid = 5093 AND unit = 'nM' AND relation = '=' AND affinity_type IN ('Ki','IC50','Kd') GROUP BY monomerid),
    b AS (SELECT monomerid, p, fy, heavy_atoms AS ha, CASE WHEN fy<=2004 THEN '2001-2004' WHEN fy<=2009 THEN '2005-2009' WHEN fy<=2014 THEN '2010-2014' WHEN fy<=2019 THEN '2015-2019' ELSE '2020-2026' END AS period,
     1.37*p/heavy_atoms AS le FROM best JOIN compound_property USING (monomerid) WHERE fy IS NOT NULL) SELECT period, count(*) AS n, median(ha) AS med_ha, median(p) AS med_p, median(le) AS med_le, round(100.0*avg((le>=0.3)::int)) AS pct_le30, min(fy) AS y0, max(fy) AS y1 FROM b GROUP BY period ORDER BY period
    
"""
await replay.call(5, 'run_sql', {'sql': sql},
                  sha256='a0475c003b9d9ca7e24b822d488955e42a2f5c5dac004a2524dce11c9387db21')

sql = """
    WITH best AS (SELECT monomerid, max(p_affinity) AS p, min(year) AS fy FROM activity

🧠 Assistant

BACE1 inhibitors became both smaller and more potent. Between the first period and 2015–2019 the median compound lost 19 heavy atoms (50 to 31) while gaining about a log unit of potency (pAffinity 6.40 to 7.38), so the median ligand efficiency rose from 0.18 to 0.33 kcal/mol per heavy atom. The most recent period (2020–2026) gives a little of that back: 33 heavy atoms, pAffinity 7.00, LE 0.30. Figure 2 shows the shift period by period.

Ligand efficiency over time

First published Compounds Median heavy atoms Median pAffinity Median LE LE ≥ 0.3
2001–2004 231 50 6.40 0.18 1%
2005–2009 918 39 6.68 0.24 7%
2010–2014 2,669 31 6.74 0.29 47%
2015–2019 5,475 31 7.38 0.33 70%
2020–2026 1,011 33 7.00 0.30 52%

LE = 1.37 × pAffinity / heavy atoms. A compound is counted once, at its best exact ('=') Ki, Kd or IC50 against human BACE1 (target 5093), in the period of its first measurement (10,304 compounds in all). 1.37 kcal/mol is the free energy of one log unit of affinity at 298 K, so LE is roughly how much binding energy each heavy atom earns.

The turn came between 2009 and 2014. The early compounds are peptidic transition-state mimetics of the amyloid precursor protein: they bind the two catalytic aspartates with a hydroxyethylamine or statine group, and they are enormous, with a median of 50 heavy atoms. The leap in the 2010–2014 period is the arrival of the cyclic amidine series (aminothiazines, aminohydantoins and the aminooxazines), which pick up the same aspartate pair with a small basic ring; the field converged on them. The table shows the size drop (39 to 31 atoms) and the LE jump (0.24 to 0.29), but not the chemistry: that attribution is from the literature, not from a BindingDB column.

The most efficient inhibitors

Ranking the compounds with a BACE1 value of 100 nM or better by ligand efficiency gives a useful warning first:

Compound Best value Heavy atoms LE LipE Source
Hydroxyethylamine (HEA) IC50 49 nM 4 2.50 7.32 PMID 21222511
CHEBI:68889 IC50 35 nM 11 0.93 6.83 PMID 33984802
US9273042, 6 IC50 0.0002 nM 30 0.58 10.58 US9273042-B2
US9273042, 1 IC50 0.011 nM 26 0.58 8.30 US9273042-B2
US9273042, 5 IC50 0.0009 nM 29 0.57 9.14 US9273042-B2

The top two are not inhibitors in any practical sense. The first is a 4-heavy-atom fragment recorded as a stand-in for the hydroxyethylamine warhead; because LE divides by heavy atoms, anything that tiny with a measurable value wins. The second, an 11-heavy-atom compound that carries a catechol PAINS alert, is the same kind of small-molecule artefact. Ligand efficiency is only comparable within a size range: pass properties: {min_heavy_atoms: 20} and the ranking becomes the one above from the third row down, which is a real series, followed by CHEMBL4083698 (IC50 2 nM, 21 heavy atoms, LE 0.57, LipE 5.57) and CHEMBL5291052 (IC50 4.7 nM, 20 heavy atoms, LE 0.57, LipE 3.54).

The record holder is a patent series. US9273042-B2 (compound 6, IC50 0.2 pM) tops the list on both counts. Patent values at the picomolar end usually come from a different assay format (here a cellular Aβ-lowering assay) than the biochemical IC50s most papers report, so treat the absolute number with care; the series is nonetheless efficient, at 0.58 kcal/mol per heavy atom.

Lipophilic efficiency ranks something else entirely. LipE = pAffinity − cLogP, which rewards potency that does not come from greasiness. Ordering by LipE alone puts the old peptides back on top: the nonapeptide NH2-Lys-Thr-Glu-Glu-Ile-Ser-Glu-Val-Asn scores LipE 13.56 at an IC50 of 30 nM, because its cLogP of about −6 inflates the difference, while its LE is 0.09. Charged, very polar molecules will always look good on LipE. The two metrics constrain different failure modes (too big, too greasy) and neither is a ranking of quality on its own.

The clinical candidates (Figure 1)

Only two BACE1 clinical candidates are recorded in BindingDB under their generic names: verubecestat (median of 4 exact values 2.1 nM, LE 0.42, LipE 7.26) and elenbecestat (median of 2 values 42 nM, LE 0.34, LipE 4.31). Both sit well inside the efficient region of the 2015–2019 panel in Figure 2. They are drawn in Figure 1 next to the patent record holder (median of its two values 1.35 nM, LE 0.49, LipE 8.52). The structure grid aligned all three on a 12-atom common core, the fluoroaryl amide arm; each also carries a cyclic amidine that binds the catalytic aspartates. Both candidates failed in phase 3, verubecestat for lack of efficacy and elenbecestat after an unfavourable risk-benefit assessment (from the literature, not from BindingDB). Efficiency metrics say nothing about whether the target is the right one.

Lanabecestat, atabecestat and umibecestat have no entry under those names at all: BindingDB records compounds under the name used in the source paper or patent, which is usually a code or a ChEMBL id.

How this was answered

  • search_targets found human BACE1 (target 5093, 10,964 compounds).
  • find_ligands_for_target with max_value_nm: 100 and order_by: "ligand_efficiency" ranked the potent inhibitors by efficiency, first without and then with properties: {min_heavy_atoms: 20}; order_by: "lipe" gave the lipophilic-efficiency ranking. Both metrics are computed from the compound_property table, which holds the RDKit heavy-atom count and cLogP of each compound's parent structure.
  • A run_sql query took each compound's best exact value and the year it first appeared, then reported the median heavy-atom count, potency and LE per period, with the share above LE 0.3. A second one returned the per-compound values (grouped by period and heavy-atom count, because run_sql returns at most 1,000 rows) for the plot.
  • The per-compound values were plotted with matplotlib and added with add_figure; search_compounds resolved the two candidates by name; draw_structure_grid drew the three structures.
